faq.a: Almost all weather happens in the troposphere, the lowest layer, which reaches about 12 kilometres up. It holds about three quarters of the air's mass and nearly all of its water vapour.
The stratosphere is the layer from about 12 to 50 kilometres up. It contains the ozone layer, which absorbs ultraviolet sunlight and makes the stratosphere get warmer with height.

faq.q: Where do shooting stars burn up?
faq.a: Most meteors burn up high in the mesosphere and just above it, around 80 to 100 kilometres up. They hit the air so fast that they heat up, glow and vaporise.
Auroras glow in the thermosphere, mostly about 100 to 300 kilometres up, where particles from the Sun strike oxygen and nitrogen atoms.
asks: How high are the northern lights?

faq.a: There is no sharp edge; the air just fades away. By common agreement, space begins at the Kármán line, 100 kilometres up.
asks: How high is the edge of space?

facts: About three quarters of the atmosphere's mass is in the troposphere.
The Kármán line, 100 kilometres up, is often used as the boundary of space.
The top of the mesosphere, around 85 kilometres up, can be colder than minus 90 degrees Celsius.

quiz.say: In which layer of the atmosphere does almost all our weather happen?
quiz.show: Almost all weather happens in the…
quiz.why: The troposphere is the lowest layer and holds nearly all the water vapour, so clouds, rain and storms happen there.

wrong.1: The stratosphere is above the weather; it is dry and calm, with the ozone layer.
wrong.2: The thermosphere is hundreds of kilometres up, where auroras glow, far above any clouds.
